newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. court hears chilling Rwanda genocide testimony.
newsitem.headline: U.N. court hears chilling Rwanda genocide testimony.

text.p: The U.N. Rwanda war crimes tribunal on Friday heard the first chilling testimony about the 1994 genocide, including descriptions of mass killings and burial alive.

A woman, identified only as "K" for her own safety, said in three hours of testimony that Hutu former government official Jean-Paul Akayesu had personally ordered the slaughter of Tutsis during the 1994 genocide.
She had worked as an accountant for Akayesu, the former mayor in Rwanda's central Taba commune. Throughout "K's" testimony, the smartly dressed Akayesu sat impassively staring at the floor.
Akayesu, 43, has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. He faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty, if convicted.
Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the U.N. tribunal for the crimes between April and June 1994, when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.

The slow-moving process has been accompanied by allegations of mismanagement and abuses by the Arusha-based court. New U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan on Thursday promised "decisive action" to clean it up.

"K" was among 31 witnesses flown at U.N. expense from the tiny central African nation of Rwanda. Presiding judge Laity Kama ordered her identity concealed throughout the trial, expected to last several weeks. Photographers and television crews were barred from the hearing to protect her.
"K" said her ordeal begun after Akayesu ordered her out of hiding in her home to the communal office on April 19, 1994, two weeks after the start of the genocide.
There she was confronted by Akayesu and a crowd of men carrying traditional weapons. Eight Tutsi men were then brought out and forced to line up on Akayesu's orders.
"The killers escorted eight people (Tutsis) right to the fence of the communal office where they were told to sit down with their arms and legs well out in front of them," she said.
"At the moment they were going to be killed they raised their arms to beg for mercy but Akayesu said 'quickly', giving the order to have them killed."

Akayesu told the Hutu extremists outside his office "go to your own sector and work", meaning to kill, she said. "K" said she was then locked up and from detention watched fellow Tutsis, including teachers, brought outside Akayesu's office and killed.
"Some were killed in very atrocious ways, while others were attacked to the point of death and then they were put in wheelbarrows and buried alive," she told the hushed court.
At midnight, Akayesu returned. She expected to die but instead he released her, "K" told the court, which will resume hearing testimony on Monday.
On Monday, Kama, head of a three-person panel of judges, will also rule on Akayesu's application to change his defence lawyers for the third time.

Twenty-one people have been indicted by the tribunal including Akayesu. Eight are still at large, seven are held in Arusha including Akayesu, four are in detention in Cameroon and the United States and Switzerland hold one each.

In a boost for the tribunal, Cameroon has signed a deal with the court to transfer to Arusha its four suspects. They include Theoneste Bagosora, a former senior army official, who Rwanda's new government says gave the military orders in the first 24 hours of the genocide.
